summary: The Link Management Protocol (LMP) was developed as part of the GMPLS protocol suite to manage traffic engineering links. This document relates LMP's procedures to discovery as defined by the ITU-T, in the context of ASON and transport network terminology, to promote common understanding. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Two groups use different words for similar ideas. This explains how one group's link-checking system lines up with the other's.

questions: what is the difference between gmpls and ason
how does lmp relate to ason
subtitle: How GMPLS link management maps to optical network discovery

tldr.problem: GMPLS (used by the IETF for optical networks) and ITU-T's ASON (used for optical networks by telecommunications) use different terminology and concepts, making it hard for the two communities to understand each other.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC explains how LMP (Link Management Protocol, part of GMPLS) relates to ITU-T's discovery work, mapping key concepts and showing where the two approaches overlap and differ.
tldr.outcome: Engineers familiar with one architecture can understand the other, enabling cooperation between IETF-based and ITU-T-based optical networks.

today: RFC 4394 remains a reference document for anyone implementing or integrating GMPLS and ASON systems. It has not been obsoleted, and the terminology mapping it provides is still used to bridge the IETF and ITU-T communities in optical networking standards work.

sections.title: Two Worlds, Different Words
sections.content:
Large optical networks are built and operated in two ways. The IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) developed GMPLS (Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching) as a control plane for routing and switching in optical and other networks. The ITU-T (a standards body for telecommunications) developed ASON (Automatically Switched Optical Networks) as a control plane for optical networks used by carriers. Both communities are working on the same problem—controlling large optical networks—but they started from different histories and developed different terminology.

This RFC is informational and bridges the two. It does not propose a new protocol or change either GMPLS or ASON. Instead, it translates the concepts so that engineers from one world can read and understand documents from the other.
sections.eli5: Two organizations invented ways to automatically manage big optical networks. They use different words for the same ideas, so this document translates between them.

sections.title: The ASON Model: Layers and Connections
sections.content:
ASON starts from a simple model of transport networks. A network has layers (different types of data: SDH timeslots, Ethernet frames, wavelengths, etc.). At each layer, there are subnetworks (sets of ports where traffic can be routed) and links (connections between subnetworks). Inside a subnetwork, connections can be flexible (set up on demand) or fixed.

ASON defines connection points (CPs) as reference points on links, and termination connection points (TCPs) as endpoints of a complete network connection. For control purposes, ASON uses subnetwork points (SNPs)—logical abstractions of connection points. The control plane uses SNPs and manages SNP-to-SNP relationships to define which traffic can flow where.
sections.eli5: Networks are organized in layers (like email vs. video). Each layer has containers of ports (subnetworks) connected by links. The control system keeps track of abstract points and which ones connect to which.

sections.title: Discovery: Transport and Control Planes
sections.content:
ASON distinguishes two discovery processes. Transport plane discovery finds which physical ports are actually connected (e.g., via G.7714.1, an ITU protocol). This is purely about the physical layer—which cables are plugged in where. Control plane discovery happens entirely in the control layer and maps control abstractions (SNPs) to physical resources.

GMPLS uses LMP (Link Management Protocol) to manage traffic engineering (TE) links. LMP has four main jobs: managing control channels (the out-of-band network where control messages flow), discovering TE link properties (what resources are bundled together), verifying physical links (checking that what you think is connected actually is), and managing faults. LMP's link verification is a control-plane operation, not transport-plane discovery like G.7714.1.
sections.eli5: First, you find out what physical ports actually connect to each other (transport discovery). Then, your control system figures out which abstract control points they correspond to (control discovery). LMP does control discovery and also checks that the wiring is right.

sections.title: Mapping: ASON Terms to GMPLS Terms
sections.content:
The RFC provides a detailed terminology mapping. A GMPLS TE (traffic engineering) link is similar to an ASON SNP link. A GMPLS port or component link maps to ASON connection points. A GMPLS data link ID (a pair of local and remote interface IDs) corresponds to an ASON CP-to-CP link name. A GMPLS link interface (with switching, termination, or adaptation capability) maps to ASON trail termination and adaptation functions.

Importantly, both systems distinguish between fixed and flexible connections. In ASON, a link connection (LC) is fixed; a subnetwork connection (SNC) is flexible. In GMPLS, component links are similar to flexible resources. The mapping is not one-to-one, but understanding these correspondences helps engineers use one system to implement the other's concepts.
sections.eli5: Here is a translation table: ASON calls something X, but GMPLS calls it Y. Once you know the translation, you can read either document without confusion.

sections.title: The Big Picture: Control Plane Architecture
sections.content:
ASON defines a three-layer functional model using Discovery Agent (DA), Termination and Adaptation Performer (TAP), and Link Resource Manager (LRM). The DA manages transport plane names; the LRM manages control plane names (SNPs); the TAP bridges them. LMP, meanwhile, is a protocol used in the control plane by GMPLS-based systems. LMP assumes IP-based control, while ASON and G.7714.1 are agnostic to the control technology.

Both systems support bundled links (many parallel links grouped as one) and hierarchical connections (an LSP in one layer can become a link in another layer). Both manage multi-layer networks and allow flexibility in how resources are advertised and reserved. However, LMP is specific to GMPLS control planes, while ASON is a general architecture that could use any control protocol.
sections.eli5: Both systems organize the control plane with agents and managers that translate between physical and logical views. LMP is one implementation of this for GMPLS; ASON is more general.

sections.title: Status and Implications
sections.content:
This RFC serves as a bridge document for standards writers and implementers who work in both camps. It shows that LMP is a valid and compatible realization of ASON control plane concepts. G.7714 (transport layer discovery) and LMP (control layer management) can coexist: G.7714.1 can discover physical adjacencies, and LMP can then verify and manage the control plane view of those links. Large optical networks may use both protocols at different layers or in different parts of the network.

The document does not create a unified system; instead, it clarifies the relationship so that a carrier using ASON can understand how GMPLS LMP fits into their architecture, and an IETF engineer can understand how ASON concepts relate to GMPLS design.
sections.eli5: This document helps two engineering communities understand each other. It shows that the two approaches are compatible and can even be used together in one big network.
